Also, that's just for VFR, meaning you're not going anywhere unless it's mostly clear.

If you want to travel with any regularity and not have to wait for perfect conditions, you'll want your MEL (multi-engine, land-based) rating, which usually also involves an endorsement for complex aircraft (i.e. retractable gear) and an instrument rating.

To get your PPL and then your MEL and IFR ratings, you're probably looking at 100+ hours (flight time, not even counting ground school and studying) and probably $30,000.

And then you're still limited to piston twins. And those can run into the 7-figure range when new. If you want to go farther and faster, you'll need a turbine rating, which lets you fly something like a King Air (twin turboprop) or a Pilatus or TBM (single turboprop). Those are....not cheap. You want a jet? That's another qualification, plus a type rating in the specific model you want to fly.
